articles.title: Spain Calls Snap Election as Housing Crisis Tests Pedro Sánchez and Socialists
articles.subtitle: Spain’s Pedro Sánchez has called a November 29 snap election as a housing crisis, political divisions and a stronger right-wing opposition threaten his Socialist government.
articles.excerpt: Spain’s Pedro Sánchez has called a November 29 snap election as a housing crisis, political divisions and a stronger right-wing opposition threaten his Socialist government.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: Housing Crisis Now the Central Issue in Election
Socialist Housing Plans Collide with Conservative Alternative
Economic Growth Does Not Relieve Political Pressure
Right-Wing Opposition Sees a Chance to Oust Sánchez
Spain’s Socialist Stronghold Put to the Test

content.text: Spain is hurtling toward an early general election after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez dissolved parliament and called voters to the polls on November 29, bringing forward a contest originally scheduled for about eight months later. The decision comes at a difficult time for Sánchez’s Socialist-led government that has struggled with a housing crisis, legislative defeats, political controversy and mounting pressure from conservative opposition parties.

Housing is the central political issue ahead of the election. Rents and house prices have become more and more unaffordable for many households and there have been repeated protests across Spain. The attempt to evict an 87-year-old woman in Madrid became a national symbol of the housing problem and helped push the issue to the center of the political debate.

Sánchez is trying to turn the crisis into an electoral advantage by framing the election as a choice between his progressive agenda and a potential right-wing government, including the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox. But the strategy is not without risk as the Socialist Party faces a tough challenge from the opposition.
Pedro Sánchez Calls Early Election

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on October 5 that Spain would hold a general election on November 29, bringing the vote forward by around eight months.The decision followed a damaging parliamentary defeat in which opposition parties blocked government measures to try to respond to the country’s housing affordability crisis.

The proposals that were defeated were intended to address issues like evictions and speculation in the real estate market. The minority government of Sánchez relies on the support of a handful of smaller parties to pass laws, making its position in parliament especially fragile. The coalition’s inability to garner enough votes demonstrated the limits of its capacity to push through major policies.

In a national address announcing the vote, Sanchez said the upcoming election was about choosing the country’s political direction. He argued that voters would have to decide whether Spain should continue with progressive policies, of social justice, openness and environmental responsibility, or turn to the political right.

Sanchez has been in power since 2018 and is now one of the longest-serving leaders in Europe. Spain has enjoyed relatively strong economic growth and job gains during his time in office, allowing the government to point to positive macro-economic indicators as evidence of his record.

But the prime minister is heading into the election with a more complicated political backdrop. His position has been weakened by corruption cases involving people close to the Socialist Party, criticism of the government’s handling of migration, and repeated parliamentary difficulties. His decision to call an early election is therefore both an attempt to regain the political initiative and a big electoral gamble.
Housing Crisis Now the Central Issue in Election

The housing shortage has swiftly gone from a long-term social problem to one of the defining issues of national politics in Spain. Housing has been a major concern for voters for several years, but recent protests and a high-profile eviction case have pushed the issue much more prominently into the political debate.

The bid to kick 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal out of her home in the Spanish capital sparked wider protests. Her building had been bought by a real estate company. The case drew nationwide attention as housing campaigners said more vulnerable residents were being exposed to rising property prices, rents and institutional investment. Then demonstrations spread throughout Spain.

The problem derives from the fact that the housing supply does not match the housing demand. Spain may have a shortfall of around one million homes by 2028. The shortage has been particularly acute in major cities and tourist areas, where demand has outpaced construction. The problem has been fueled by bureaucratic delays, a lack of construction workers, short-term rentals, and demographic changes.

Young people have been especially impacted. Some 73% of Spaniards own homes, but a large majority of those aged between 18 and 34 live with or depend on their parents for housing or financial support. House prices have also risen much faster than wages, making it harder for young workers to get into the housing market.

Another layer to the problem is the limited social housing stock in the country. Social housing represents just 1.7% of the total housing stock in Spain, according to European Commission calculations, far below levels in many other European countries.
Socialist Housing Plans Collide with Conservative Alternative

Housing policy is likely to be a key line of division between Sánchez’s Socialist Party and the conservative opposition ahead of the November election. The Socialist government has implemented measures like rent controls and limitations on certain corporate purchases of real estate. Those measures were rejected by right-wing lawmakers, who said they could discourage investment and reduce the supply of new homes.

The opposition People's Party, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, is proposing another option. Feijóo has promised to help build 250,000 houses a year and speed up urban planning processes to free up more land for development. His proposals include beefed up mortgage and rental guaranties for younger people.

Competing strategies reflect a wider debate about the causes of Spain’s housing shortage. Socialists have instead concentrated on protecting renters and cracking down on practices; they say are driving up housing costs. Conservatives argue that the best way to rein in prices is to increase supply and warn curbs on property investors could deter construction.

However, whichever way it goes, experts see major complications. Spain is a very decentralized country. Although the central government can set up national legislation and incentives, regional governments and municipalities have major responsibilities for carrying out housing policy and urban planning.

That split has made housing reform especially difficult. Measures proposed by successive governments have sometimes been blocked, rejected, or not fully implemented. This has created a persistent gap between the political promises and the homes actually coming forward in areas of highest demand.

So, the election will see voters pitted against competing accounts of the crisis. Sánchez can argue for stronger protections for tenants and more public intervention, while Feijóo can campaign on construction, deregulation and increasing supply.
Economic Growth Does Not Relieve Political Pressure

Sánchez comes into the election with an economic record that is stronger than the political mood may imply. Spain's economy has grown faster than many of the large eurozone economies since the pandemic, while employment is at its highest level since 2008. But those gains haven’t stopped increasing frustration over household budgets and cost of living.

Spain’s gross domestic product rose by 2.8% in 2025 and is expected to grow by around 2.4% in 2026. Hence, the country’s economic performance post-pandemic has been relatively strong by European standards. Tourism, job creation, and immigration have all helped fuel the expansion.

The problem for Mr. Sánchez is that headline economic growth has not been translated evenly into better living standards. Productivity is a worry, with output per employee and per full-time worker not growing much. A big chunk of the jobs creation was concentrated in the relatively low productivity sectors.

Inflation has added to the pressure. Inflation was running at around 5% in September, well above the eurozone average. Higher fuel costs and package holiday prices were among the factors behind the rise. Higher costs can make broader economic growth seem less relevant to households already feeling the squeeze on housing costs.

Housing has emerged as the most glaring example of the disconnect between national economic performance and individual experience. While many young workers in Spain are unable to buy homes or afford independent rental accommodation, the country can boast stronger GDP and employment figures.

That tension could define the campaign. Sánchez will try to put the focus on economic growth and jobs, but the opposition can say that the benefits of that growth have not been translated into enough improvement in everyday living standards. The housing crisis allows conservatives and other opposition parties to turn macroeconomic success into a political liability by highlighting affordability.
Right-Wing Opposition Sees a Chance to Oust Sánchez

The snap election allows the conservative People's Party and the far-right Vox to take on Sanchez's Socialist government in a time of political uncertainty.The People's Party already has the largest number of seats in parliament, and polling showed the party ahead of the Socialists.

Feijóo has greeted the early election, casting the contest as a chance to oust Sánchez. His campaign is expected to focus on housing, but also on allegations of corruption around figures close to the Socialist Party and criticism of the government’s handling of migration.

Vox could play an important role if the right wins enough support to form a government. A defeat for Sánchez could open the door to a coalition of the conservative People’s Party and Vox, which would represent a major shift in the direction of Spanish politics.

But the Socialists are trying to transform the election into a broader ideological battle. Sanchez has warned voters of what he calls a wider far-right political wave in Europe and is presenting his government as a defender of social justice, openness and progressive policies.

The political battle is therefore likely to spill over into housing. Immigration, corruption, public services and Spain’s stance on international issues are also likely to take center stage. Sanchez has developed an international reputation as a progressive leader in Europe, but domestic opponents have increasingly homed in controversies surrounding his government.

Spain’s fragmented parliament means that even a strong result for one party does not automatically translate into a government. Coalition talks and deals with smaller parties could again decide who will ultimately control the government.

The election is therefore not just a referendum on Sánchez personally. It will also decide whether Spain stays with a progressive coalition or turns to a center-right led government, maybe with the backing of the far-right.
Spain’s Socialist Stronghold Put to the Test

The vote on November 29 will be a big test for Sánchez and the Socialist Party after years in government. His central political argument is that voters are faced with a choice between sticking to Spain’s progressive course or veering right. But the severity of the housing crisis means that voters may hold the government more accountable for whether life has become more affordable in everyday life.

Spain’s housing crisis has laid bare a contradiction at the heart of Sánchez’s record. The country has enjoyed relatively strong economic growth and job gains, but housing costs have risen rapidly, and affordable accommodation has become more difficult, especially for young people.

The protests show the extent of the problem. Tens of thousands took to the streets demanding action, and demonstrations went on after Sánchez announced his election. In Barcelona, protests over housing turned into clashes with police, who reported arrests and injuries among officers.

The timing of the election is an attempt by Sánchez to capitalize on the political momentum around housing before other controversies come to the fore. The vote gives the opposition an opportunity to transform anger at housing, corruption, and government management into a shift in power.

The outcome might have implications beyond Spain. Sánchez’s government is one of the main left-of-center governments in Europe, and a change to a conservative government backed by Vox would shift the political balance in the European Union. Spain may be a crucial test for the rest of Europe’s progressive political forces.

The campaign is expected to center around housing, economic conditions, political stability, and the country’s broader ideological direction with the election set for Nov. 29. Ultimately, it will be up to Spanish voters to decide if Sánchez can turn the housing crisis into a case for another progressive term — or if that same crisis is what ends his government’s time in office.

articles.title: Flydubai captain describes opening cockpit door after co-pilot attack
articles.subtitle: Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi how he opened the cockpit door after being attacked by his co-pilot during a flight to Tel Aviv.
articles.excerpt: Captain Smit Machchhar recounted the mid-air attack on Flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the rapid descent of more than 14,000 feet, and the decision that let passengers and crew intervene.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: Flight dives thousands of feet during attack
Passengers help retake control of plane

content.text: Captain Smit Machchhar of Flydubai has described how he managed to open the cockpit door after being attacked by his co-pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, enabling passengers and crew to intervene as the plane dived.

Machchhar spoke to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a video call on October 2 from a hospital in Abu Dhabi, where he is recuperating from injuries. He appeared with bandages on his head and hands and described the moments he realized the aircraft was losing altitude.

The captain said he had collapsed to the cockpit floor after being hit several times. As the plane descended, he realized that opening the cockpit door could give others a chance to reach the attacker and help regain control. He said he got to the door and opened it while still being attacked. Passengers then entered the cockpit and helped subdue the co-pilot.
Machchhar said he had been flying for 17 years and a captain for 11 years. His account was the first detailed public description of the incident from the injured captain himself.
Flight dives thousands of feet during attack

The incident took place aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 on Wednesday as the Boeing 737 flew from Dubai to Tel Aviv. Tracking data showed the aircraft lost more than 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds during the cockpit emergency.

Reports on the number of people on board varied slightly. The Associated Press reported 182 people including eight crew members; Reuters reported that Machchhar told Modi the plane had 174 people on board.

The co-pilot allegedly assaulted Machchhar inside the cockpit before the rapid descent. Motive remained unclear as authorities investigated. Passengers rushed in and helped subdue the attacker. A second group of pilots who were traveling on the flight later helped take control of the aircraft.

The plane was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and made an emergency landing. Authorities in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Israel are investigating, with U.S. and Omani authorities also assisting, according to the Associated Press.
Passengers help retake control of plane

Machchhar's decision to open the cockpit door presented an opportunity for passengers to step in. Witnesses said passengers entered the cockpit and helped restrain the co-pilot while the plane was still in trouble. After the attacker was subdued, other pilots on board helped steady the flight. The aircraft eventually landed safely in Tabuk.

One passenger said he went into the cockpit during the descent and helped pull the aircraft's controls up. The attacker was also restrained by other passengers. The episode has drawn attention because aviation security systems are typically designed to keep unauthorized people out of the cockpit; here the perceived threat came from inside the cockpit itself.

Investigators are examining how the attack unfolded and whether it was linked to terrorism or advance planning, the Associated Press reported. UAE prosecutors have launched an inquiry into the circumstances and potential motive. Israeli officials said the alleged assailant, an Omani national, was arrested after the emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. His motive has not been publicly identified.
Authorities investigate; pilot recovering
Machchhar is recovering in hospital in Abu Dhabi. India's embassy and consulate officials have been in touch with his family while authorities coordinated with counterparts in the UAE.

In his conversation with Modi, Machchhar became emotional recalling the incident. He said he knew he had to get back up because if the aircraft kept going down, passengers could die. "During the crisis, I recited Hanuman Chalisa and it gave me courage when I was injured," Machchhar told the prime minister.

Modi praised the captain's actions and wished him a speedy recovery. Officials in India, the UAE and Israel have publicly acknowledged the actions of Machchhar and the passengers who intervened. At the same time, investigators are working to determine precisely how the cockpit attack took place and why it happened. The UAE attorney general has ordered an investigation into the circumstances and any link to terrorist activity or advance planning.

The case may prompt aviation authorities to review procedures for identifying and responding to threats involving crew members. Aviation security systems have traditionally focused heavily on preventing passengers or outsiders from gaining access to cockpits. For now, Machchhar remains hospitalized as the inquiry continues. The immediate emergency was averted with the safe landing of Flight FZ1073.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet border flood: what is known and what remains uncertain
articles.subtitle: Later official figures sharply raised the toll after the Bhote Koshi disaster, while access and communications complicated the count
articles.excerpt: A source-based update on the Bhote Koshi flood, the changing casualty estimates and the recovery questions facing remote Himalayan communities.
articles.author: admin

content.text: A destructive flood moved through the Bhote Koshi border corridor on August 26 after a high-mountain slope failure and temporary river blockage. The surge damaged transport links, settlements and energy infrastructure in difficult terrain. Early official counts were incomplete because roads and communications were cut.
How the event unfolded

Reports from the first days described a mass of ice and rock entering a tributary above the border corridor, temporarily holding back water before a surge traveled downstream. Precise attribution in a remote high-altitude catchment takes time: satellite analysis, field access and hydrological records all contribute, and early explanations should not be treated as a final scientific assessment.
Why the numbers changed

On August 27, authorities were reporting at least 390 deaths and about 1,400 people missing across affected areas. By September 7, Nepal's disaster management agency said more than 1,300 people had died and roughly 5,000 were missing, according to the Associated Press. The later figures supersede the headline counts in the first version of this post.

A missing-person total is not the same as a confirmed death toll. Displaced residents, damaged phone networks and incomplete local registers can all enlarge the number of people who are temporarily unaccounted for. The figures should therefore be read with their dates and sources attached.
The longer recovery

Immediate work centered on rescue, shelter, medical care and restoring access. Recovery also raises longer questions about bridge design, warning systems and development in narrow valleys exposed to landslides and glacial hazards. Nepal's government issued an international relief appeal, while health authorities published response updates for affected districts.

This post was updated on September 9 to replace early casualty estimates with later figures and to make the uncertainty around missing-person counts explicit. The linked official notices and subsequent assessments should be consulted for further changes.

articles.title: Iran and Oman propose temporary shipping corridor through Strait of Hormuz
articles.subtitle: The plan aims to restore navigation through mine clearance and phased traffic rules
articles.excerpt: Iran and Oman have outlined a phased framework for a temporary joint shipping corridor and a mine-clearing mission through the Strait of Hormuz, even as President Trump says the U.S. Navy has already cleared the waterway's main channel and traffic has surged as Tehran's grip on the strait weakens.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: Iran's weakening grip on the strait

content.text: Iran and Oman have outlined a phased framework for a temporary, jointly managed shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, along with a mission to clear mines from the waterway, marking one of the clearest steps yet toward restoring full commercial navigation through the critical passage after months of disruption.
What the proposal includes

Oman's foreign minister, Badr al-Busaidi, traveled to Tehran to meet his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, where the two described their talks as constructive and released a joint statement outlining what they called "a phased framework that could provide a practical and implementable basis for moving forward." The framework includes establishing a temporary joint navigational corridor through the strait and a joint project to clear mines from it, with al-Busaidi saying afterward that he hoped the two countries would "soon announce" the corridor and practical arrangements to restore safe navigation. A permanent solution and long-term governance of the strait, the statement said, would follow later.

Iran has insisted that inbound ships use a northern route through its own territorial waters, while the U.S. military has spent months protecting tankers using a separate southern route that hugs Oman's coastline. U.S. Central Command has said more than 660 million barrels of crude oil have exited the strait under its protection along that southern corridor since May, even as sporadic attacks on shipping in the region continued, including two cargo ships struck last week in an incident that killed two sailors.
Conflicting claims on the mines

The proposed mine-clearing mission was announced the same day President Trump said on social media that the U.S. Navy had already removed or detonated all mines from the strait's international waters, warning that Iran had been notified that any vessel caught laying new mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed." Axios reported that U.S. officials corroborated the claim, saying the Navy had spent months using underwater drones to scan the strait's median shipping lane, identifying more than 100 suspected mines that private contractors were then hired to remove or destroy. Oman's reference to a still-pending mine-clearing mission appeared to sit uneasily alongside Trump's announcement, and it remains unclear how the two efforts relate.
Iran's weakening grip on the strait

The diplomatic overture comes as Iran's practical control over traffic through the strait has eroded sharply. Weekly vessel transits have surged from around 40 two weeks ago to nearly 200 more recently, with more than 80% of liquid cargo shipments either using the U.S.-backed Omani corridor or moving without transponders, likely along the same southern route Tehran has rejected. One oil-market analyst described the shift bluntly, saying it increasingly looks as though Iran has at least partially lost control of the strait. The strait became a flashpoint after war broke out earlier this year between Iran, the United States and Israel, and the current negotiations build on a June memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran aimed at ending that conflict. Qatar has voiced support for the talks, with its prime minister expected to travel to Tehran for follow-up discussions, and news of the proposed framework helped push oil prices lower for a third straight session as traders weighed the prospect of more Gulf crude reaching global markets.

articles.title: New UK prime minister abolishes science and technology department in Whitehall shake-up
articles.subtitle: Lawmakers warn the reorganization could fragment policy on artificial intelligence and research funding
articles.excerpt: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has dissolved the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, folding most of its responsibilities into a new business department while moving artificial intelligence policy directly into the Cabinet Office, a move that has unsettled parts of Britain's tech sector.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, dissolving the three-year-old ministry as part of a wider reorganization of Whitehall carried out shortly after he took office.
What changed

The department, created in 2023 by then-prime minister Rishi Sunak to bring science, technology and digital policy together under one roof, will see most of its functions absorbed into a newly formed Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, while responsibility for digital transformation and online harms moves instead to the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The government has framed the change as a way to align technology policy more closely with economic strategy, arguing that folding research and innovation into the business department will produce a more coordinated national industrial strategy and reduce duplication across government.
Who moved where

Jonathan Reynolds, who previously led the old business department before serving as chief whip, has returned to lead the new combined department, which inherits the Sovereign AI investment unit, the Advanced Research and Invention Agency and UK Research and Innovation, bringing research funding and commercialization policy under one roof for the first time. Artificial intelligence policy has been elevated rather than folded in: Kanishka Narayan, appointed minister of state for artificial intelligence, will work jointly across the Cabinet Office and the new business department and will attend cabinet meetings, a first for the AI brief. The AI Security Institute is expected to remain closely tied to the Cabinet Office as part of that arrangement. Liz Kendall, the outgoing science secretary who helped establish the Sovereign AI Fund, stepped down before the reshuffle was formally announced, as did Lord Patrick Vallance, the science minister and former government chief scientific adviser.
Reaction from the tech sector

The decision has unsettled parts of Britain's technology and investment community. In an open letter published before the reshuffle was confirmed, the industry groups TechUK and the Startup Coalition warned that the old department gave the sector "a single government partner that understands it," and that folding it into a larger structure risked diluting attention to fast-moving areas like artificial intelligence and life sciences just as momentum was building. Supporters of the change counter that embedding science and technology policy directly inside the government's economic engine room, rather than keeping it siloed in a standalone department, will make it easier to translate research into commercial growth. Parliament's own science and technology committee has said it expects to hear directly from ministers in the coming weeks about how the transition will be managed and which parts of government will take the lead on ongoing initiatives, including the country's AI adoption plans.

articles.title: Typhoon Dolphin slams China's coast as region endures busy storm season
articles.subtitle: The storm was the most powerful to hit the country so far this year
articles.excerpt: Typhoon Dolphin made a double landfall in eastern China's Zhejiang province with winds near 94 miles per hour, prompting the evacuation of more than a million people and the cancellation of over 1,300 flights as the region endures its most active typhoon season in years.
articles.author: admin

toc.text: Part of an unusually active season

content.text: Typhoon Dolphin made a double landfall on China's eastern coast in Zhejiang province on the evening of August 9, arriving as the most powerful storm to hit the country this year and triggering the highest level of typhoon alert issued by China's National Meteorological Center.
Landfall and mass evacuations

The storm first came ashore near Yuhuan in Taizhou with maximum sustained winds of roughly 151 kilometers per hour, or about 94 miles per hour, equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane, before making a second landfall in nearby Yueqing about 70 minutes later. Authorities evacuated more than a million people across the region, including roughly 900,000 residents relocated in the city of Wenzhou alone, where more than 1,000 emergency shelters were opened, along with about 390,000 people evacuated in Taizhou and tens of thousands more in Shanghai and neighboring Fujian province.

Coastal cities including Wenzhou, Taizhou and Ningbo activated Level I emergency response, the highest tier in China's four-level system, with Wenzhou ordering a citywide suspension of classes, work, production and transportation. Air travel across the region was badly disrupted, with Shanghai's Pudong and Hongqiao airports canceling more than 1,300 flights and Hangzhou's airport canceling nearly 400 more. Ferry and cruise services across Zhejiang and Fujian were suspended, and authorities in Fujian relocated construction crews and vessels away from offshore project sites as a precaution.

Search and rescue crews searched for a nine-year-old boy swept into the sea during the storm in the city of Wenling, according to local media. Forecasters warned that parts of Zhejiang could see 200 to 400 millimeters, or up to nearly 16 inches, of rain as Dolphin moved inland, raising the risk of flooding and landslides in mountainous areas. The storm continued tracking westward into central China in the days that followed, prompting Beijing to raise its own rainfall warnings and prepare to activate its flood control response.
Part of an unusually active season

Dolphin was the thirteenth named typhoon of the year in the northwest Pacific and the second storm this season to trigger China's highest-level red alert, following Typhoon Noul in late July. Forecasters have described the season as unusually active across the basin, in contrast to a comparatively quiet Atlantic hurricane season, with China, Japan and the Philippines all struck by separate storms in rapid succession earlier in the summer. The storm arrived within days of a separate tropical system that brought heavy rain to Hawaii, illustrating the wide geographic reach of this year's active Pacific storm pattern.
